summary:
Kuala Lumpur is a federal territory. The national Penal Code applies directly in the territory, and the Federal Territories Sharia criminal enactment, which criminalises cross-dressing and same-sex conduct, operates alongside it, enforced by the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi). Jawi carries out operations jointly with the Kuala Lumpur police and Kuala Lumpur City Hall. The Sharia offences bind Muslims; non-Muslim visitors are exposed to the Penal Code alone.

On 28 November 2025 police, Kuala Lumpur City Hall and Jawi raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit and arrested 208 men under section 377B of the Penal Code, the largest such operation since 2022. Media were tipped off in advance, and detainees' faces and personal details were published. Seventeen civil servants among those arrested were suspended from their posts.

A magistrate refused the police request to extend remand, finding that no case had been made out under section 377B, but release was still delayed; at one point more than 130 detainees remained in custody, among them 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid.

Venue enforcement in the territory predates the sauna operation: a Kuala Lumpur gay bar was raided in August 2018.

In July 2020 the minister responsible for the Federal Territories said Jawi had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons. The International Commission of Jurists called for the order to be revoked.
tangentialFactors:
The national-level response to the Chow Kit operation came on 2 December 2025, when the Home Minister said the provisions would be revisited; within days police raided another sauna in Penang. The sources record no amendment following that statement.

Legal challenges have not removed the framework. The Federal Court struck down a Selangor cross-dressing provision in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024, but on federalism grounds about which legislature may enact the offence rather than on the substance, and nothing under the Penal Code was decriminalised. A challenge to the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing was denied by the High Court, leaving the Federal Territories enactment under which Kuala Lumpur prosecutions proceed in place.
localsOnly:
Muslim residents of Kuala Lumpur fall under the Federal Territories Sharia enactment as well as the Penal Code, and Jawi enforcement in the territory is directed at them; non-Muslim residents are not subject to the Sharia offences.

Employment consequences follow arrest: 17 civil servants arrested in the November 2025 sauna operation were suspended from their posts.

Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters, in a report published in August 2022 based on interviews with 73 LGBT people between 2018 and 2021, including Kuala Lumpur residents, documented state-backed discrimination against LGBT people. A Kuala Lumpur activist quoted in the report described a regression as a conservative strand of Islam gained ground.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not record what charges or prosecutions followed the 208 arrests of 28 November 2025, beyond the refused remand and the releases.

Whether the July 2020 ministerial statement of licence remains in force is not sourced.

The Federal Territories Sharia enactment contains no legal definition of transgender dress; the boundary between compliant and offending presentation is set by officers, and no published guidance defines it.

No territory-level count of violence against transgender people with a population denominator was identified, so no rate specific to Kuala Lumpur can be stated.

Litigation over gender-marker changes on identity cards, including the 2016 Kuala Lumpur High Court order requiring the National Registration Department to update a trans man's card and its reversal on appeal in 2017, concerns the national registration regime rather than a rule specific to the territory.
